To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1. MFDE and MFPSO are able to improve the performance on all 9 single objective optimization problems, compared with the corresponding monofactorial versions.
(1) MFPSO and/or MFDE are competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms on the MFO benchmark problems, and (2) MFPSO/MFDE is a promising alternative for multi-objective MFO.

(1) MFO can be implemented in different population based search mechanisms, (2) MFO can significantly enhance the search performance in terms of convergence characteristics and (3) MFPSO is the best performing algorithm for MFO.
In summary, our research is concerned with
two main questions: (1) how does MFO perform when it is combined with two popular population based search mechanisms, namely PSO and DE, respectively?
the following two questions: (1) Can MFO be successfully implemented by using different population based search mechanisms?
the following questions: Q1. Can the proposed MFPSO and/or MFDE achieve competitive performance against the state-of-the-art MFO algorithms on MFO benchmark problems?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed MFPSO and MFODE are both effective and efficient in solving the MFO benchmark problems.
the proposed multifactorial PSOs and DEs outperform their single factor counterparts on most problems.

MFPSO and MFO are both effective in solving single objective optimization problems, and the proposed MFPSO and multifactor DE algorithms are able to outperform their corresponding single tasking variants in terms of convergence speed and solution quality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MFO is indeed a powerful approach for evolutionary multi-optimization, and it can be successfully applied to a wide range of search algorithms.
MFPSO and MFO are comparable, but MFPSO is more stable.

MFO is not only a promising approach for improving convergence characteristics across multiple problems, but it can also be applied to other popular population based search mechanisms, such as PSO and DE.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the proposed multifactorial PSOs and DEs are able to outperform the corresponding single objective PSOs and DE, respectively, on most of the benchmark problems, which demonstrates the potential of MFO to improve convergence performance of population based search mechanisms.
MFO is indeed generalizable and can be readily combined with other search mechanisms.
MFO can be successfully employed with different population based search algorithms and it is not limited to a particular search mode.
